question: P is any point inside the rectangle ABCD. If PA = 87 cm, PB = 12 cm and PC = 96 cm, then the length of PD (in cm) is equal to:
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

For any point P inside a rectangle ABCD, the sum of the squares of distances to opposite vertices is equal.

PA² + PC² = PB² + PD²

87² + 96² = 12² + PD²

7569 + 9216 = 144 + PD² ⇒ 16785 = 144 + PD²

PD² = 16785 − 144 = 16641 ⇒ PD = √16641 = 129 cm.

**∴ The correct answer is 129 cm.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

• P A B C D 87 12 96 PD = ? 

**Given:**

PA = 87 cm

PB = 12 cm

PC = 96 cm

**Formula Used:**

According to the **British Flag Theorem**, if P is any point inside a rectangle ABCD, then the sum of the squares of distances from P to opposite vertices is equal. Therefore:

PA² + PC² = PB² + PD²

**Calculations:**

⇒ 87² + 96² = 12² + PD²

⇒ 7569 + 9216 = 144 + PD²

⇒ 16785 = 144 + PD²

⇒ PD² = 16785 − 144

⇒ PD² = 16641

⇒ PD = √16641

⇒ PD = 129 cm

**∴ The correct answer is 129 cm.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

British Flag Theorem

This geometric theorem states that for any point P chosen on the plane of a rectangle ABCD (whether inside or outside the boundaries), the relation PA² + PC² = PB² + PD² always remains completely valid.

Proof by Pythagoras Theorem

This property can be logically proven by drawing perpendiculars from point P to all four sides of the rectangle. This process forms four smaller right-angled triangles, enabling the direct application of the Pythagoras theorem: a² + b² = c² on opposite segments to yield the result.

General Rectangle Properties

In any standard rectangle, opposite sides are necessarily equal and parallel. Additionally, the diagonals are perfectly equal in total length and bisect each other, intersecting securely at the absolute center point.
